articles.title: BepiColombo begins Mercury arrival with MTM separation success
articles.description: On 3 September 2026 at 15:49 CEST, the European Space Agency's BepiColombo Mission Control Team at the European Space Operations Centre (ESOC) received the signal they had been waiting for – BepiColombo’s Mercury Transfer Module (MTM) successfully separated from the spacecraft stack. This landmark achievement for the ESA and Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) mission marks the first step of BepiColombo's long-awaited arrival at Mercury.
articles.summary: BepiColombo successfully completes its magnetometer tripod module separation, a critical milestone in its arrival sequence at Mercury. This achievement represents a major step toward one of the most ambitious planetary science missions in history.

articles.title: Roman lifts off on a mission to survey the infrared sky
articles.description:
Image:
			
NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope lifted off on a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket from NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida, USA, at 07:26 EDT / 12:26 BST/ 13:26 CEST on 30 August 2026. With the successful launch, Roman began its mission to survey the sky in visible to near-infrared light to help reveal the nature of dark energy and dark matter. The telescope will also investigate the true diversity of exoplanets in our galaxy.
Roman is a NASA-led mission to which the European Space Agency (ESA) contributed star trackers, batteries, and detectors for the coronagraph instrument. ESA will also provide communications support through its deep-space ground station network, and enable data download using its new 35-metre antenna in New Norcia, Australia.
“I warmly congratulate our colleagues at NASA on the successful launch of Roman,” says Carole Mundell, ESA’s Director of Science. “ESA is proud to have provided essential hardware and to continue supporting Roman’s ambitious scientific goals. Together, we are opening new windows on the cosmos.”
Like ESA’s Euclid space telescope, Roman will enable astronomers to study the Universe in unprecedented detail. It is equipped with a primary mirror of 2.4 m and two instruments: the Wide Field Instrument (WFI) and a Coronagraph Instrument technology demonstration.
With its panoramic view of the sky, crisp infrared vision and quick re-orientation skills, Roman will perform fast and efficient surveys of a large area of the sky. By doing so, it will map clustering of galaxies over time and space and also study the light coming from thousands of distant type Ia supernovas which will help astronomers trace the expansion of the Universe.
“Roman should provide our clearest picture yet of whether dark energy is truly constant or whether it evolves over cosmic time – either outcome would have profound implications for our understanding of the Universe. I'm also excited by Roman's exoplanet census, which will discover thousands of new worlds, including cold planets and free-floating planets that have remained largely beyond our reach until now,” says Bethan James, ESA’s Roman Project Scientist. “Perhaps what excites me most is the unexpected. With its unprecedented combination of depth, area, and image quality, Roman has every opportunity to surprise us.”
After launch, Roman is on a steady course to the second Sun-Earth Lagrange point (L2), nearly 1.5 million km away from Earth. This location allows the telescope to have an unobstructed view of a wide area of the sky, almost 12%. Like ESA’s Euclid and the NASA/ESA/CSA James Webb Space Telescope, Roman will move in a wider orbit around the L2 point – much larger than the Moon’s orbit around Earth.
In the next three months following launch, the Roman team will conduct a carefully orchestrated series of deployments, calibrations, and tests. Once the commissioning period is complete, the mission will begin its science operations, starting with the first science image release. Roman will spend at least five years scanning the infrared sky and is designed to work in space for another five years.
[Image description: A SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket with NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope on board is seen transiting the Sun during launch from Launch Complex 39A, on Sunday 30 August 2026, at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida, US.]
articles.summary: NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope successfully launches aboard a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket, beginning its mission to survey the infrared sky. This landmark achievement represents a major advancement in space-based astronomy and technology partnership.

articles.title: Watch live: BepiColombo begins its arrival at Mercury
articles.description:
After eight years, the ESA/JAXA BepiColombo mission is about to enter its Mercury Arrival Phase. On 3 September 2026, ESA’s Mercury Transfer Module (MTM) will separate from BepiColombo’s two science orbiters – the first major step in one of the most operationally challenging planetary arrival sequences ever attempted by ESA.  
The European Space Agency (ESA) will livestream the critical milestone from 13:45 CEST. Tune in and witness the first step of one of the most complex phases of the mission, live from ESA mission control.  
Join ESA's livestream on YouTube here!
articles.summary: The ESA/JAXA BepiColombo mission prepares for its historic arrival at Mercury after eight years of travel, marking a major milestone in planetary exploration.

articles.title: Japan's Hayabusa2 Achieves First-Ever Laser Ranging Experiment with an Asteroid
articles.description: On Sunday July 5th, 2026, the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) achieved the first-ever successful laser ranging experiment while making a flyby of an asteroid.
articles.summary: Japan's Hayabusa2 spacecraft successfully conducts the first-ever laser ranging experiment on an asteroid, demonstrating innovative space exploration techniques.

articles.title: Extremely massive galaxy proto-supercluster smashes distance record
articles.description: An international team of astronomers has discovered the most distant progenitor to a galaxy supercluster ever. The discovery supports existing theories of how galaxy clusters evolve and reveals how they are connected to the larger cosmic web. The study relies largely on data from the ODIN survey, conducted with the U.S. Department of Energy-fabricated Dark Energy Camera on the U.S. National Science Foundation Víctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope in Chile.
articles.source: Space News - Space, Astronomy, Space Exploration
articles.summary: Astronomers discover the most distant galaxy supercluster progenitor ever observed, setting a new record and revealing the universe's early structure.

articles.title: Scientists observe Einstein’s gravity in the quantum world for the first time
articles.description: Physicists have directly observed a long-predicted quantum effect of gravity, putting one of Einstein’s foundational ideas to a striking new test. Using ultracold atoms, researchers split an atom’s quantum wave so that one part was held in place while the other fell freely under gravity, then reunited the two to measure the tiny difference that emerged.
articles.summary: Physicists have directly observed a quantum effect of gravity predicted by Einstein, validating a fundamental theory at the intersection of quantum mechanics and general relativity.

articles.title: Is it a planet or a moon? Scientists discover a strange Jupiter-sized world orbiting a brown dwarf in a never-before-seen cosmic system
articles.description: Astronomers found a massive object orbiting a brown dwarf star. This discovery challenges existing definitions of planets and moons. The unusual system features a nested orbital arrangement unlike our solar system. Scientists are debating the object's classif…
articles.summary: Astronomers discovered a Jupiter-sized object orbiting a brown dwarf star in an unprecedented cosmic system, challenging our understanding of planet and moon definitions.

articles.title: Rocky planets were expected to become common only after generations of stars enriched the universe over billions of years. But simulations show that a powerful early supernova could seed a disk with several Earth masses of planetesimals just 100 million years after the Big Bang—less than one percent of the universe’s current age.
articles.description:
A simulated Population III supernova remnant produced enough concentrated solids for rocky-world precursors at cosmic dawn, but the calculation stopped well before a finished planet.
The post Rocky planets were expected to become common only after generations…
articles.summary: Simulations demonstrate that a powerful early supernova could have seeded rocky planet precursors just 100 million years after the Big Bang, suggesting planets formed far earlier than expected.

articles.title: Curiosity Blog, Sols 4995-5001: 5,000 (Martian) Days on Mars
articles.description: Written by William Farrand, Senior Research Scientist, Space Science Institute Earth planning date: Friday, Aug. 28, 2026 The span of sols spanned by this blog post is noteworthy in several ways. First, Curiosity became a world-class (for Mars at least) mountaineer by passing the 1 kilometer mark of elevation from its landing site on the floor […]
articles.summary: NASA's Curiosity rover celebrates 5,000 Martian days of exploration on Mars, marking a remarkable milestone in planetary science. The rover continues to advance our understanding of the Red Planet's geology and potential for past habitability.

articles.title: NASA Calls for Proposals to Accelerate Lunar Surface Technologies
articles.description: NASA is seeking proposals to advance the technology and infrastructure needed to explore the Moon and establish a Moon Base in the lunar South Pole region. Announced on Tuesday, Sept. 8, the solicitation targets capability gaps, including power generation, oxygen extraction, and producing materials on the Moon required for construction and operations. These technologies are […]
articles.summary: NASA seeks innovative proposals to advance lunar surface technologies and infrastructure for establishing a sustained Moon base. This initiative represents a critical step toward long-term lunar exploration and scientific discovery.

articles.title: Superbubble in the Large Magellanic Cloud
articles.description: NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope captures a photogenic nebula, N44, in the Large Magellanic Cloud in this Sept. 3, 2026, image. N44 is dominated by two features: a vast central void and a shell of dense, dusty gas. The central void is a ‘superbubble’ spanning roughly 210 by 140 light-years across. The glittering stars at the […]
articles.summary: NASA's Hubble Space Telescope captures stunning images of superbubble N44 in the Large Magellanic Cloud, revealing massive stellar structures and stellar feedback processes. This observation provides insights into star formation and galactic evolution.

articles.title: NASA’s Hubble, Webb Find Far-out Solar System Objects ‘Remember’ Past
articles.description: For the first time, scientists used the joint power of NASA’s Hubble and James Webb Space Telescopes to study some of the most far-flung bodies in our solar system, Trans-Neptunian Objects (TNOs). Some of these are the smallest and faintest ever directly seen. The researchers unexpectedly found fewer small TNOs than they expected, and that […]
articles.summary: NASA's Hubble and James Webb Space Telescopes collaborate to study distant solar system objects, revealing surprising preservation of their orbital history. This joint observation demonstrates the power of combining multiple space observatories for deeper cosmic insights.

articles.title: BepiColombo’s Mercury arrival begins - full replay
articles.description:
Video: 
			02:31:10
				
Watch the replay of the livestream originally broadcast on 3 September as ESA/JAXA's BepiColombo mission took the first critical step towards arriving at Mercury.
After travelling through the inner Solar System together for eight years, BepiColombo's Mercury Transfer Module (MTM) will separate from the rest of the stacked spacecraft on 3 September 2026. This marks the beginning of one of the most complex planetary arrival sequences ever attempted by ESA.
Broadcast live from ESA's European Space Operations Centre (ESOC) in Darmstadt, Germany, the programme includes live views from the iconic Main Control Room, expert analysis, behind-the-scenes insights, and the first signal from the spacecraft following separation. 
Livestream schedule (CEST): 

13:45 – Livestream begins 
16:00-16:45 – End of livestream
articles.summary: The ESA/JAXA BepiColombo mission livestream captures the excitement of Mercury arrival operations. This public broadcast celebration demonstrates international collaboration in advancing solar system science.

articles.title: Hubble tracks new decagon encircling Saturn’s south pole
articles.description: Recent observations with the NASA/ESA Hubble Space Telescope have revealed a giant, evolving 10-sided atmospheric wave encircling Saturn’s south pole. This discovery marks the first time a large regular-sided jet pattern has been observed in the planet’s southern hemisphere. The feature appears remarkably similar to Saturn’s famous hexagon at its northern pole, but is also distinctly different, suggesting scientists may be witnessing a new atmospheric phenomenon develop on the iconic gas giant.
articles.summary: Hubble observations reveal a giant, evolving 10-sided atmospheric wave pattern encircling Saturn's south pole. This discovery enhances our understanding of Saturn's complex atmospheric dynamics and planetary science.

articles.title: Icy Exocomets Around a Distant Star Help Explain Earth's Water
articles.description: Did icy comets deliver water to the young Earth? That idea won't go away. Now, astronomers at Lund University in Sweden have found evidence of exocomets orbiting a young star named PDS 70. The observations suggest that these comets are delivering water to that system's inner regions.
articles.summary: Astronomers discover icy exocomets around a distant star that provide new insights into how water may have been delivered to early Earth.

articles.title: Scientists Are Still Trying To Understand How the Moon Formed
articles.description: The Earth and the Moon have nearly identical isotopic compositions, and the Giant Impact Hypothesis strives to explain this. New research into the ancient impact shows how the temperature of both worlds, and how it affects the strength of the materials involved in the collision, shaped the outcome, including the isotopic compositions.
articles.summary: Scientists continue investigating the Giant Impact Hypothesis to explain how the Moon formed, using isotopic composition analysis to unlock lunar origins.

articles.title: Some Black Holes Grow Much Faster Than Their Galaxies
articles.description: New observations find that a few supermassive black holes are unexpectedly large given the size of their galaxies. This suggests the connection between black holes and galaxies isn't as strong as we thought.
articles.summary: New observations reveal that some supermassive black holes grow unexpectedly large relative to their host galaxies, challenging current understanding of black hole formation.

articles.title: A New Mission Could Rendezvous With Halley's Comet In 2061
articles.description: Halley’s comet captures the imagination in a way that few other astronomical objects do. When it last made its approach toward the Sun (admittedly when this author, who is now middle-aged, was one year old in 1986), humanity responded with a fleet of spacecraft known informally as the “Halley Armada”. Yet, because of the comet’s trajectory, those spacecraft were only able to visit their target for a fleeting few hours, leaving planetary scientists wanting more. Now, a new paper by researchers at Khalifa University and their co-authors, and available in pre-print on arXiv, describes a mission plan that would allow a spacecraft to actually rendezvous with this most well-known comet for the first time ever.
articles.summary: A proposed mission aims to rendezvous with Halley's Comet during its 2061 appearance, opening new possibilities for studying this iconic celestial object.

articles.title: Do Black Holes Grow Along With the Universe? A New Study Says Yes
articles.description: We know the universe is constantly expanding. We also know that gravitationally bound objects, such as solar systems and black holes, seem to be immune to that expansion. But a new paper, available in pre-print on arXiv by theoretical physicists Valerio Faraoni and Massimiliano Rinaldi challenges that assumption. They suggest that black holes can’t just ignore the expanding universe around them. Instead they have to expand along with it.
articles.summary: A new study suggests that supermassive black holes grow in proportion with the expanding universe, providing fresh insights into cosmic evolution.

articles.title: Fast radio bursts could help disentangle galactic feedback from dark matter effects
articles.description: Intense, brief flashes of radio light called fast radio bursts (FRBs) travel across billions of light-years to reach Earth, passing through a fog of matter along the way. The bursts' origins are unclear but may originate from highly magnetized dead stars called magnetars. The denser the fog through which FRBs travel, the more dispersed their signals become—similar to the way a prism splits white light into a rainbow of colors.
articles.source: Space News - Space, Astronomy, Space Exploration
articles.summary: Fast radio bursts offer a powerful new tool for distinguishing dark matter effects from galactic feedback processes across billions of light-years.

articles.title: Martian air could yield methane rocket fuel with fewer unwanted byproducts
articles.description: As NASA prepares to send humans to Mars as early as the 2030s, University of Mississippi researchers are working on one of the key questions: How will they get back?
articles.source: Space News - Space, Astronomy, Space Exploration
articles.summary: University of Mississippi researchers develop methods to extract methane fuel from Martian atmosphere with minimal byproducts, supporting NASA's human Mars missions planned for the 2030s.

articles.title: Quiet black holes with a stellar companion raise questions about how they form
articles.description: Active black holes are easy to detect. Their superheated accretion disks emit bright X-rays, and the jets streaming from their poles are easily seen at visible and radio wavelengths. But most stellar-mass black holes are inactive. They either drift through the galaxy alone or orbit a companion star without consuming its material. We can't observe inactive black holes directly. We can only observe their effects on nearby objects. We currently know of three such black holes thanks to the Gaia spacecraft.
articles.source: Space News - Space, Astronomy, Space Exploration
articles.summary: Observations of quiet black holes with stellar companions provide new clues about black hole formation mechanisms, expanding our understanding of these cosmic objects.

articles.title: Hubble and Webb find that far-out solar system objects 'remember' the past
articles.description: For the first time, scientists used the combined power of NASA's Hubble and James Webb Space Telescopes to study some of the most far-flung bodies in our solar system, trans-Neptunian objects (TNOs). Some are the smallest and faintest ever directly seen. The researchers unexpectedly found fewer small TNOs than expected and that the colors of these bodies followed the same relationships as those of their larger family members.
articles.source: Space News - Space, Astronomy, Space Exploration
articles.summary: Hubble and James Webb Space Telescopes combine their power to study distant solar system objects, revealing how they retain memories of the early solar system's formation.

articles.title: NASA scientists discover a giant 10-sided pattern on Saturn
articles.description: A huge 10-sided atmospheric pattern has appeared around Saturn’s south pole, giving the planet a surprising counterpart to its famous northern hexagon. Hubble data suggest the strange decagon only began emerging in the past few years and is still growing stronger. Researchers hope continued observations will reveal why it suddenly formed and whether it could persist for decades.
articles.summary: NASA scientists discover a striking 10-sided atmospheric pattern around Saturn's south pole, revealing unexpected geometric structures in the gas giant's dynamic atmosphere.

articles.title: The universe has plenty of hydrogen. So why is star formation collapsing?
articles.description: Star formation across the universe has fallen dramatically over the past 4.5 billion years, but astronomers have uncovered a surprising twist: the supply of neutral hydrogen, a key ingredient for making stars, has barely declined. Using China’s FAST radio telescope and data from roughly 2.5 million galaxies observed by DESI, researchers found that star formation was about 2.5 times higher 4.5 billion years ago, while neutral hydrogen levels were only about 1.4 times higher.
articles.summary: Astronomers investigate why star formation has declined dramatically over the past 4.5 billion years despite abundant hydrogen, uncovering mysteries about cosmic evolution.

articles.title: Deep beneath Mars, scientists find a vast hidden magma system
articles.description: Deep beneath Mars, scientists have found evidence of enormous magmatic systems once thought to require Earth-like plate tectonics. Seismic measurements suggest molten rock repeatedly evolved and recycled itself through the Martian crust, potentially across hundreds or thousands of kilometers. The discovery challenges long-held ideas about how complex planetary crusts form.
articles.summary: Scientists discover vast hidden magma systems deep beneath Mars' surface, revealing the Red Planet once possessed Earth-like geological processes.

articles.title: Stoke Space raises $1 billion for fully reusable rockets, targets 'early 2027' for 1st-ever launch
articles.description: Stoke Space announced a $1 billion round of funding to support development of its fully reusable Nova rockets, including the newly revealed Nova Block 2, which will be capable of delivering 15-ton payloads to low Earth orbit.
articles.summary: Stoke Space secures $1 billion in funding to develop fully reusable Nova rockets, targeting an early 2027 launch for a groundbreaking spaceflight innovation.

articles.title: NASA Scientists Discover Giant 10-Sided Pattern on Saturn’s South Pole
articles.description: NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope has detected a massive, evolving 10-sided atmospheric wave circling Saturn’s south pole, according to a study published Sept. 3, 2026, in the journal Science Advances. The finding, reported by NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center, …
articles.summary: NASA's Hubble Space Telescope discovered a massive 10-sided atmospheric wave circling Saturn's south pole, offering scientists a rare opportunity to observe an unusual and evolving cosmic phenomenon.

articles.title: Rubin Observatory Peers Deep Into the Famous COSMOS Field
articles.description: A new image from NSF–DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory offers a spectacularly deep view into a famous region of sky known as the COSMOS field.
articles.summary: The Vera C. Rubin Observatory captured a spectacularly deep image of the famous COSMOS field, revealing unprecedented detail of distant galaxies and cosmic structures.

articles.title: In 1974, humans sent their first message to the stars from a radio telescope in Puerto Rico, aimed at a cluster 25,000 light-years away
articles.description:
On 16 November 1974, the Arecibo radio telescope in Puerto Rico transmitted humanity's first deliberate interstellar message toward the M13 star cluster — a 1,679-bit binary picture that will not arrive for 25,000 years.
The post In 1974, humans sent their fi…
articles.summary: On November 16, 1974, humanity transmitted its first deliberate interstellar message from the Arecibo radio telescope in Puerto Rico, aimed at a star cluster 25,000 light-years away.
